newsitem.title: UK: Mark crosses subdued amid overall mark weakness.
newsitem.headline: Mark crosses subdued amid overall mark weakness.

text.p: The mark's tone against its European counterparts was subdued in morning trade, dampened by the mark's across-the-board weakness.

Any rise in the mark against the lira, following a cut in key Italian interest rates on Friday, was quashed as the German currency sank against the British pound, dollar and yen, led by sterling/mark's surge to its highest level in five years.

"Mark weakness against sterling and the dollar, the UK budget and the FOMC later this week -- all this is bubbling under the surface, and so the mark/lira rally on the rate cut didn't really happen," said one trader at a Japanese bank here.

Mark/lira was at 976.05/45 at 0955 GMT, down slightly from the 977.40/60 seen in late European trade on Friday before the Bank of Italy trimmed its discount and Lombard rates by half a point to 6.25 and 7.75 percent respectively.
Traders said market reaction to the rate cut was muted also because it had been long anticipated, and the size of the reduction was smaller than expected, with many expecting 75 basis points.
"We can't see a clear reason why (Bank of Italy governor Antonio) Fazio waited so long and why the cut was so small," said one trader at an Italian bank here.

"People are speculating that it could have been that he (Fazio) wanted more certainty about whether Italy was going to join EMU, to avoid a confusing situation like cutting rates then having to raise them again," the trader said.
The extent of the rate cut was smaller than expected, but analysts said they were not looking for another before the Italian budget this autumn.

"A lot of the reforms in Italy have been cosmetic rather than structural, and the Bank of Italy wants to see something done on the structural side," said Tom Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.
"I think we need to see some real efforts made on budget reform before the Bank of Italy cuts rates again," he said.
Meanwhile, the market was unruffled by a growing rift within Germany over adherence to EMU entry criteria.

Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber -- a senior member of the Christian Social Union which is a partner in the ruling coalition -- insisted monetary union should be delayed if candidate members could not fulfill the criteria.

"It's one of those debates that has been running for some time, and the market's getting a bit weary with it because it never seems to come to a head," said Glenn Davies, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
The market would be unable to react decisively on the issue until next month, when an audit of France's public finances and Germany's budget are due to be presented, Davies said.

For the most part, the market was still convinced the will to launch EMU would still prevail, analysts said. Stoiber's stance could also have a political base, they said, citing rivalry between him and German finance minister Theo Waigel.
But some added this did not mean his words were unrealistic.

"Stoiber's going against the political drive towards EMU by mentioning the unmentionable, but what he says makes sense," said SocGen's Rayner. "He doesn't want a watered-down euro, he's saying a relaxed interpretation (of the criteria) is bad news and it's not doing the German economy any good."
